title: Episode 7: The Defenestration of Prague: The Seventy-Foot Fall That Ignited a Continent
description:
On May 23, 1618, enraged Protestant Bohemian nobles stormed Prague Castle and hurled two royal imperial governors and their secretary out of a high chancery window. Falling seventy feet, all three survived by landing in a massive pile of stable waste—triggering the Thirty Years' War.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. History has an uncanny way of pivoting upon moments of sheer absurdity that spiral into unimaginable human tragedy. In May of sixteen eighteen, a bitter religious dispute inside the Holy Roman Empire reached its boiling point in the high council chambers of Prague Castle in Bohemia. A group of armed Protestant aristocrats decided to resolve an imperial treaty dispute using an ancient Bohemian custom: they picked up the Emperor's royal regents and hurled them out of a third-story window. What happened during that seventy-foot drop—and the miraculous, foul-smelling heap that caught them—ignited the Thirty Years' War, one of the bloodiest conflicts in human history. Here is George with the story.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: THE LETTER OF MAJESTY
In the opening years of the seventeenth century, the Kingdom of Bohemia was an island of delicate, uneasy religious peace within the Holy Roman Empire. Nearly ninety percent of the Bohemian population belonged to Protestant traditions—predominantly the Hussites, spiritual heirs of the fifteenth-century martyr Jan Hus, alongside German Lutherans and Calvinists. Yet, their crowned king was the Catholic Habsburg Emperor residing in Vienna. To prevent civil war in his realm, the eccentric Emperor Rudolf II had established his imperial court in Prague, surrounding himself with alchemists, painters, and astronomers like Johannes Kepler. In sixteen-oh-nine, under intense pressure from the Bohemian Diet, Rudolf signed the celebrated Letter of Majesty. This imperial charter guaranteed the Protestant nobility absolute freedom of religion and the legal right to construct their own churches, cemeteries, and schools. For a brief decade, Bohemia enjoyed an unprecedented era of religious coexistence. In sixteen seventeen, however, the political landscape darkened catastrophically. The aging, childless Emperor Matthias arranged for the Bohemian crown to pass to his cousin, Archduke Ferdinand of Styria. Ferdinand was a hardline Catholic crusader, educated by the Jesuits at Ingolstadt, who had sworn an oath before the Virgin Mary to eradicate heresy from all his realms, even if it reduced his lands to a smoking desert. Almost immediately, imperial authorities began violating the Letter of Majesty. In the northern towns of Broumov and Hrob, Catholic officials closed newly built Protestant churches, tearing one to the ground and locking the doors of the other. When Protestant estates submitted a formal legal petition of protest to Emperor Matthias in Vienna, the response was a furious imperial decree. The Emperor denounced their assembly as unlawful and treasonous, strictly forbidding further meetings and threatening the organizers with severe criminal prosecution.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE SECRET MEETING AT SMIŘICKÝ PALACE
The Protestant nobles were thoroughly convinced that the Emperor's blistering letter had not originated from Matthias in Vienna, but had been drafted locally in Prague by his most reactionary Catholic regents. Chief among these imperial governors were Count Jaroslav Borzita of Martinitz and Count Vilem Slavata of Chlum—two zealous Catholic converts who had famously refused to sign the Letter of Majesty nine years earlier. On the stormy evening of May twenty-second, sixteen eighteen, prominent Protestant leaders gathered in urgent, clandestine council at the Smiřický Palace, nestled beneath the walls of Prague Castle in the Lesser Town. The dominant voice belonged to Count Jindrich Matyas Thurn, a fiery, battle-hardened nobleman who had spent decades commanding cavalry against the Ottoman Turks in Hungary. Thurn possessed a thunderous voice, an imposing military bearing, and an absolute contempt for legalistic petitions. He argued passionately that humble appeals to the Habsburg court were futile exercises in surrender. Against royal absolutism, only swift and decisive violence could safeguard their constitutional liberties. Thurn proposed a radical and terrifying measure: they would march en masse upon the royal castle the following morning, confront the imperial governors face-to-face, and dispose of Martinitz and Slavata using traditional Bohemian defenestration. In Bohemian political history, defenestration was not common murder; it was a recognized political act of popular justice. In fourteen nineteen, during the Hussite Wars, an angry mob had thrown Catholic town councilors out of the New Town Hall windows onto spears below. Thurn reminded the nobles that by committing an irrevocable act of violence, the Bohemian estates would burn their bridges with the Habsburgs. They would have no choice but to unite, take up arms, and defend their ancient liberties.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: STORMING THE CHANCERY
On the tense morning of May twenty-third, sixteen eighteen, a cold spring mist hung low over the spires and red-tiled roofs of Prague. An armed delegation of several dozen Protestant nobles, knights, and burghers, led by Count Thurn, climbed the steep stone ramp of Hradcany Castle. Wearing black velvet cloaks, wide-brimmed hats, and carrying rapiers and concealed wheel-lock pistols, the nobles strode unchallenged through the outer palace courtyards and into the Louis wing of the Royal Palace. They ascended the winding stone stairs to the third-floor council chancery, pushing open the heavy carved oak doors. Inside sat four imperial governors and their young clerk, Philip Fabricius. Count Thurn stepped forward and ordered the two moderate Catholic regents, Count Diepold of Lobkowitz and Adam of Sternberg, to leave the room immediately, assuring them that no harm was intended toward them. The two men quickly withdrew, leaving Martinitz and Slavata alone to face a room packed with fifty armed enemies. The council chamber erupted into furious shouting. Thurn brandished the Emperor's threatening letter, demanding to know whether Martinitz and Slavata had personally advised the Emperor to threaten the Protestant assembly. Martinitz replied with cold aristocratic arrogance, stating that the governors were accountable only to the Emperor in Vienna, and that their advice was an imperial secret. Thurn turned to the assembled nobles and shouted: 'Were we to keep these men alive, we would lose the Letter of Majesty and our heads! The time has come to act as our ancestors did!'

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: THE SEVENTY-FOOT DROP
Chaos erupted inside the council chamber. Four muscular nobles seized Martinitz, pinned his arms behind his back, and dragged him across the room toward an open window overlooking the castle moat seventy feet below. Martinitz cried out in terror: 'Jesus, Son of the Living God, have mercy on my soul! Mary, Mother of God, protect me!' Ignoring his frantic prayers, the nobles hoisted him over the stone sill and hurled him headfirst into the abyss. The crowd then turned its fury upon Count Slavata. Slavata fought back with ferocious desperation, clawing at the window frame with both hands. A Protestant knight drew a heavy steel hunting dagger and struck Slavata repeatedly across his knuckles and fingers, breaking his grip until blood smeared the stone sill. Slavata lost his hold and plunged backward into the seventy-foot drop, striking his head against a stone cornice as he tumbled. Standing in the corner of the room, the young imperial secretary, Philip Fabricius, was cowering beneath an oak desk, trembling in fear. The nobles hauled Fabricius out by his collar. Despite the clerk's desperate pleas that he was merely a humble scribe carrying out official orders, the mob tossed him out the window behind his employers. As the three bodies tumbled through the morning air toward the rocky moat seventy feet below, one of the Protestant conspirators leaned over the ledge and mocked them loudly: 'Let us see if their Virgin Mary can catch them now!'

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: THE MIRACLE OF THE DUNG HEAP
A seventy-foot plunge onto hard stone flagstones or jagged rocky crags is almost invariably fatal to the human body. When the Protestant nobles peered out of the high chancery window, expecting to see three mangled corpses lying in pools of blood, they were greeted by an astonishing sight. All three men were alive, moving, and scrambling across the ground. For generations, palace cooks, stable boys, and chancery staff had routinely dumped decomposing straw, kitchen refuse, and horse manure directly out of the council windows onto the steep slope of the castle ditch. Over decades, this organic waste had formed a colossal, soft, and spongy mountain of dung and compost that absorbed the kinetic energy of their fall. Martinitz had struck the center of the deep manure pile feet-first, emerging virtually unscathed except for torn breeches and bruised shoulders. Slavata had suffered a severe concussion and head wound from hitting the stone cornice, but he too had rolled safely into the soft mulch. The nimble clerk, Fabricius, had landed on his feet like an agile cat on the edge of the pile. From the window high above, Protestant guards began discharging their wheel-lock pistols into the moat, bullets kicking up clouds of dust and dirt around the fallen regents. Displaying remarkable courage, Martinitz lifted the bleeding Slavata and dragged him into the shelter of the adjacent palace gardens and the townhouse of Countess Polyxena of Lobkowicz, who sheltered the wounded men and refused entry to armed Protestant search parties. Looking down from the chancery window, the Protestant noble who had mocked their faith muttered in bewildered disbelief: 'By God, their Mary has helped them after all!' The Catholic Church immediately proclaimed their survival a divine miracle, declaring that angels and the Virgin Mary had caught the men in mid-air. Protestant propagandists retorted with biting satire, publishing widely circulated pamphlets asserting that the Catholic governors had survived simply because they had landed in their natural element: a giant heap of manure.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE THIRTY YEARS' CATASTROPHE
What began as an absurd, slapstick defenestration in a castle moat rapidly metastasized into the most horrifying human catastrophe of early modern Europe. The clerk Philip Fabricius slipped out of Prague disguised as a traveling servant, riding south to Vienna to deliver firsthand news of the rebellion to the imperial court. In gratitude for his dramatic ordeal and loyalty, Emperor Ferdinand II knighted Fabricius, bestowing upon him the hereditary title Baron von Hohenfall—literally, the Baron of the High Fall. In Prague, the Protestant estates formed a revolutionary directory, renounced their allegiance to Ferdinand, and offered the Bohemian crown to the young Calvinist ruler of the German Palatinate, Elector Frederick V. Frederick accepted, becoming known as the 'Winter King' because his reign would last barely one single season. In sixteen twenty, an imperial and Catholic League army of twenty-seven thousand veteran soldiers marched into Bohemia under Count Tilly. On November eighth, sixteen twenty, at the Battle of White Mountain just outside Prague, the imperial forces shattered the demoralized Bohemian army in less than two hours. Frederick fled into lifelong exile, and the Bohemian rebellion was crushed. Yet, the conflict did not end; instead, it consumed the entire European continent. The war drew in Denmark, Spain, Sweden under warrior-king Gustavus Adolphus, and Catholic France under Cardinal Richelieu, fighting against the Austrian and Spanish Habsburgs. For thirty agonizing years, vast mercenary armies roamed Central Europe, living off the land, burning thousands of villages, and spreading plague, typhus, and catastrophic famine. By the time the Peace of Westphalia was signed in sixteen forty-eight, over eight million people had perished. Nearly one-third of the population of the German lands and Bohemia had been wiped off the face of the Earth—all tracing its spark to three men tumbling into a castle dung heap.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE EXECUTION ON OLD TOWN SQUARE
For the Kingdom of Bohemia, the aftermath of the rebellion was nothing short of national extinction. Emperor Ferdinand II took merciless vengeance upon the land that had defied him. He revoked Rudolf's Letter of Majesty, tearing the document in half before the imperial court, and declared Bohemia an absolute, hereditary Catholic dominion. On June twenty-first, sixteen twenty-one, twenty-seven leaders of the Protestant rebellion—nobles, knights, scholars, and prominent magistrates—were brought to a massive, black-draped wooden scaffold erected in Prague's Old Town Square. Before an immense and silent crowd surrounded by ranks of imperial soldiers, the royal executioner, Jan Mydlář, carried out the bloody sentences using four different broadswords. Twenty-four men were systematically beheaded, including the celebrated humanist scholar and university rector Jan Jesenius, whose tongue was torn out before his head was struck from his shoulders. Three other conspirators were hanged from the town hall balcony. Twelve of the severed heads were placed inside iron cages and hoisted to the top of the Old Town Bridge Tower of the Charles Bridge, where they remained exposed to the sun, wind, and rain for ten years as a macabre warning to the populace. The ancient Protestant nobility of Bohemia was completely eliminated. Their vast estates were confiscated and distributed to foreign Catholic generals and mercenaries from Italy, Spain, and Wallonia. Tens of thousands of Protestant families were forced to choose between conversion to Catholicism or permanent exile into the German states. The Defenestration of Prague had begun as a bold, theatrical assertion of constitutional liberties, but it ended by extinguishing Bohemian independence for three hundred years.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
The Defenestration of Prague stands as history's most terrifying warning of how political spectacle can spark uncontrollable catastrophe. A moment of theatrical anger, meant to assert Bohemian liberties, ended up turning an entire continent into an ash heap for thirty years. Thank you for listening to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Join us next time for another forgotten chapter of history. Until then, stay curious.
